newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Cano Limon woes send U.S. refiners shopping.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cano Limon woes send U.S. refiners shopping.

text.p: U.S. refiners are shopping around for crude oil alternatives to Colombian Cano Limon in the wake of yet another series of rebel attacks on the Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline, traders said on Monday.
But the market is considered adequately supplied currently, precluding a major effect on prices.

"There isn't such a big impact. What seems to be happening is that there's plenty of crude in the system," a South American seller of competing crudes said, adding that they had only received one or two requests for prompt crude from affected buyers.

At least two major buyers, Amoco Corp and Exxon Corp, have been probing the market for prompt deliveries of similar grades since last week, when Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol declared force majeur on liftings, oil traders said.
Force majeure has been in place since the morning of July 6.
Amoco bought two 500,000 barrel cargoes of Cano Limon last month from Elf Aquitaine and Coastal. The cargoes are due to co-load at Covenas on the tanker "Alta" on July 22-26.
As a result of the shutdown, the vessel is not expected to load until sometime after July 28, traders said.

Cano Limon is a medium- to heavy-gravity crude with an API gravity of 29.5 degrees and a low sulfur content of 0.47 percent. Similar regional crudes include Mexican Isthmus, Venezuelan Lagotreco, Mesa, Furrial and Guafita and Argentine grades such as Escalante and Canadon Seco, traders said.
Cano Limon is currently priced around $2.30 a barrel under West Texas Intermediate/Cushing for August loading.

The Cano Limon oil field, which had been producing around 180,000 barrels per day (bpd), remained shut in on Monday, four days after leftist rebels dynamited the pipeline leading to the Caribbean port of Covenas.
Although such bombings are commonplace in Colombia, continued security problems in the region have prevented the Colombians from repairing the 250,000 bpd, 774 kilometer line.
Meanwhile, a two-million barrel floating storage unit moored 16 kilometers off Covenas is close to depletion, traders said, keeping incoming vessels from loading.
A spokesman for Occidental Petroleum Corp, which operates the field, cited ongoing concerns about regional security and he could not say when operations would resume.

"Cano Limon remains shut in. There's some genuine concern about the deteriorating security situation in general. We have also received reports that there have been other breaches in the pipeline that have not even been investigated up to this point," the spokesman said.
"There is some concern about the whole question of public order deteriorating in the outlying regions and questions about issues relating to territorial control," he said.

"This is a situation that's going to have to be evaluated over the coming days and weeks in terms of what types of countermeasures are going to be necessary" to restart production and keep it going, he said.

The pipeline has been blown up 37 times so far this year. All of the attacks are thought to be the work of National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels, who dynamited the pipeline 47 times last year and spilled more than 105,000 barrels of crude.
